title: How to pass this in a day
blurb: What the paper is, what it is set from, and the order to take it in.

blocks.label: The paper, and where it comes from
blocks.html:
One paper, two halves, three hours. An objective section and a theory section, sat together.

The theory is three questions and there is no choice

Question 1 from Module One. Question 2 from Module Two. Question 3 from Module Three.
Nothing can be skipped, because there is nothing to skip to. A paper offering three of four lets you abandon a topic; this one does not.

Each theory question carries a practical. Modules Two and Three are almost entirely diagram work, so expect to draw: a use case diagram, an ERD, a class diagram, a sequence or activity diagram.

The objective section follows test 2's format, which is not what most people prepare for. Test 2 was an even three-way split:

FormShare of test 2What it costs you

Single MCQ10 of 30The familiar one
Matching10 of 30One wrong pair often drags a second with it

title: The Analyst, and What Analysis Is
blurb: Module One Unit 1. Who the analyst is, the eight-step problem-solving approach, and the skills the job needs.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto: Cover the page below the first line. Read a frame, answer the question, then slide down one line to check.

frames.teach: System analysis is the systematic process of studying an existing or proposed system to understand its structure, functions, processes and interactions, so you can identify problems, determine requirements, and recommend improvements.
frames.ask: In one word, what is analysis trying to produce an understanding OF?

frames.check: the problem, or the existing system.
frames.teach: Said more sharply, it is the process of understanding and specifying in detail what an information system should accomplish. Notice the word: WHAT.
frames.ask: So does analysis say what the system must do, or how it will do it?

frames.teach: System design is the other half: translating the requirements identified during analysis into a detailed blueprint for building the system. It defines how the system will be structured, how its components interact, and how it operates.
frames.ask: Analysis asks what. Design asks which one-word question?

frames.teach: The manual is blunt about the order: what needs to be done must be defined first; how it will be done is not important yet. Getting that backwards is the commonest failure in the whole subject.
frames.ask: Who is the person who does all this?

frames.teach: A systems analyst is a professional who investigates, analyses and evaluates an organisation's information systems and business processes, to design or improve systems that support organisational goals. The short version the manual gives: a systems analyst is a problem solver.
frames.ask: The analyst sits between which two groups?

frames.check: business users and technical development teams.
frames.teach: That link role is the whole job: ensuring business needs are accurately translated into technical specifications. Everything else follows from standing in the middle.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: the seven roles, and the eight steps
blocks.html:
The seven roles and responsibilities of a systems analyst.

RoleWhat it involves
Requirements analysisGathers, analyses and documents user and system requirements using structured techniques
System evaluationStudies existing systems to identify problems, inefficiencies and areas for improvement
Feasibility studiesAssesses technical, economic, operational, legal and schedule feasibility
System modelling and documentationPrepares models such as DFDs, Use Case Diagrams and ERDs
Liaison roleHandles communication between stakeholders to ensure mutual understanding
Solution recommendationProposes solutions including hardware, software and process improvements
Support during development and implementationAssists in design, testing, user training and deployment
The analyst's approach to solving problems, all eight steps in order

1. Research and understand the problem
2. Verify that the benefits of solving it outweigh the costs
3. Define the requirements for solving it
4. Develop a set of possible solutions (alternatives)
5. Decide which solution is best, and make a recommendation
6. Define the details of the chosen solution
7. Implement the solution
8. Monitor to make sure you obtain the desired results

Step 1 has three parts the examiner asks for by name: who is involved, what business processes come into play, and what other systems would be affected by solving the problem.

Choosing between alternatives: the challenge is to select the best, meaning the solution with the fewest risks and most benefits.

Design specifications describe the construction details of all system components: databases, networks, program modules, operating procedures, user interfaces, and conversion plans. Six items, and the last one covers the changeover, not the software.

Build on bad requirements and you get: over budgeting, late delivery, or a system that does not fully solve the problem it was meant to address.

blocks.label: Systems, subsystems, and the word decomposition
blocks.html:
Three definitions that stack on each other.

Learn these three as a set

A SYSTEM is a collection of interrelated components that function together to achieve some outcome.
An INFORMATION SYSTEM is a collection of interrelated components that collect, process, store and provide as output the information needed to complete business tasks.
Or: an arrangement of people, data, processes and information technology that interact to do the same.

What an information system is for: to process input, maintain data, produce reports, handle queries, handle online transactions, and generate other outputs.

A SUBSYSTEM is a system that is part of another system. A sales management system might be a subsystem of a customer relationship management system.

Dividing a system into components this way is called FUNCTIONAL DECOMPOSITION, and it is what lets the analyst focus on one area of a business, a group of related areas, or the interfaces between areas.

Hold onto that word. It returns in Module Two as levelled DFDs, where one process becomes an entire diagram of its own, and it appears in Module One's principles as divide and conquer. Same idea, three names.

What analysis is all about, in the manual's own three bullets: understanding the business and its goals and strategies; defining requirements for information systems that support those goals; and supporting the business. Its purposes are to ensure the system meets user and organisational needs, reduce the risk of system failure, provide a clear foundation for design and development, and improve efficiency, accuracy and decision-making.

blocks.label: The three kinds of skill
blocks.tag: and which one the manual calls most important
blocks.html:
An analyst needs technical, business and people knowledge. The manual is explicit about the ranking, and it is not the one most students expect.

Interpersonal skills are the analyst's MOST IMPORTANT skills

Because analysts rely on managers, users, programmers, technical specialists, customers and vendors to take a system from idea to implementation. And because people are the source of requirements information, the labour that builds systems, and the ultimate users of it.

The analyst is a translator, in three directions: business objectives into functional requirements, user needs into system specifications, and technical jargon into terms non-technical people understand.

The six fundamentals an analyst should understand:

  • Computers and how they work
  • File, database and storage hardware and software
  • Input and output hardware and software
  • Computer networks and protocols
  • Programming languages, operating systems and utilities
  • Communication and collaboration technology, such as digital telephones, videoconferencing and web-based document management
Tools against techniques, a favourite distinction

TOOLS are software products used to develop analysis and design specifications and completed system components.
TECHNIQUES are strategies for completing specific system development activities.

Tools: software packages such as Microsoft Access, IDEs such as Oracle JDeveloper and Microsoft Visual Studio, and computer-aided visual modelling tools such as Rational XDE Modeller and Visible Analyst.
Techniques: project planning, cost/benefit analysis, interviewing, requirements modelling, architectural design, network configuration, and database design.

Business knowledge means knowing what business functions organisations perform, how they are structured, how they are managed, and what work goes on in them; and about the specific company, what it does, what makes it successful, what its strategies and plans are, and what its traditions and values are.

blocks.label: Every test question on this unit
blocks.tag: 5 of the sixty, answered and explained option by option

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: Test 1 Q16 asks what the analyst must do FIRST, and every wrong option is a genuine later step in the same eight-step sequence. Confirming benefits outweigh costs is step 2. Developing alternatives is step 4. Design specifications come at step 6. They are all real; only one is first. When a question says FIRST, it is testing the ORDER, not the content.

blocks.label: Drill every fact in this unit
blocks.tag: 50 questions from the course text, every option explained

blocks.big: "Analysis says WHAT, design says HOW, and the analyst is a problem solver standing between users and technical teams."
blocks.sub: Eight steps, starting with understand the problem. Seven roles. Six technologies. Tools are products, techniques are strategies. And interpersonal skills matter most, because people are the source, the labour and the users.

lead: Analysis says what, design says how, and the analyst is the problem solver standing between users and technical teams.

title: The System Development Life Cycle
blurb: Module One Unit 2. Nine principles, predictive against adaptive, and the five phases with their activities and deliverables.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page, read a frame, answer, then slide down to check.

frames.teach: The entire process of building, deploying, using and updating an information system is called the systems development life cycle, the SDLC.
frames.ask: Does the SDLC stop when the system is delivered?

frames.check: no. Using and updating are part of it.
frames.teach: There are two overall approaches. A PREDICTIVE approach assumes the process can be planned and organised in advance and the system built to that plan, moving through a fixed sequence of phases, each completed before the next begins.
frames.ask: What kind of system does predictive suit?

frames.check: one that is well understood and well defined.
frames.teach: An ADAPTIVE approach assumes the project CANNOT be planned in full in advance and must be modified as it goes. It handles changing requirements and uncertainty by working in short cycles with continuous user feedback and incremental delivery.
frames.ask: What is the short cycle called?

frames.teach: Each sprint produces a working version of the system or a system component. Not a document. Not a phase. Something that runs.
frames.ask: Name the example the manual gives of an adaptive model.

frames.teach: In a predictive approach the four activity groups are project planning (planning, organising, scheduling), analysis (understanding the problem, defining requirements), design (program structure and algorithms), and implementation (programming, testing, installing).
frames.ask: Those four are called phases. What is the fifth phase?

frames.teach: And here is the detail the examiner likes: support is part of the overall SDLC but is NOT normally considered part of the initial development project. It covers upgrading and maintaining the system after deployment.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: the nine principles of successful systems development
blocks.html:
Nine of them, and test 1 asked about four. Learn the name AND the reason, because the questions quote the reason.

PrincipleWhy, in the manual's terms
Get the user involvedRequirements are accurate, resistance to change is reduced, user acceptance increases
Use a problem-solving approachSolve real business problems rather than merely applying technology: understand, evaluate alternatives, select greatest benefit with least risk
Establish phases and activitiesStructure and control, so projects are easier to manage, monitor and evaluate, each step finished before the next
Establish standards for development and documentationConsistency, quality and clarity, making systems easier to understand, maintain and enhance over time
Justify systems as capital investmentsSystems need significant money, so evaluate them like any capital investment with cost-benefit analysis against costs and risks
Do not be afraid to cancel or revise scopeIf it becomes too costly, risky, or misaligned, revising or cancelling prevents further waste
Divide and conquerBreak a large system into smaller manageable components to simplify development and reduce complexity
Design systems for growth and changeFlexible and scalable for business expansion, new technology and changing requirements, which extends useful life and protects the investment
Proper planning and project managementOn schedule, within budget, meeting quality: realistic timelines, resources, risk, progress monitoring

A memory hook for the order: the first two are about ATTITUDE (involve users, solve problems), the next three about DISCIPLINE (phases, standards, justification), and the last four about JUDGEMENT (know when to stop, break it up, plan for change, manage the work).

blocks.label: Predictive against adaptive, the table the exam wants
blocks.tag: four rows, learn them as pairs
blocks.html:
Predictive approachAdaptive approach
Requirements are defined upfrontRequirements evolve over time
Development follows a linear and structured sequenceDevelopment is iterative and incremental
Emphasis on detailed documentationStrong user involvement and collaboration
Limited flexibility to accommodate changesEmphasis on working systems over extensive documentation

The adaptive phases, which are not the same as the predictive five:

  • Initiation and requirements planning: high-level scope, the business problem, objectives, key stakeholders and major features. Detailed requirements are deliberately NOT fully specified. Requirements are captured at a high level and prioritised by business value and urgency, often as user stories or feature lists
  • Iterative analysis and design: only the requirements selected for the current iteration are analysed and designed in detail
  • Iterative development or construction: each iteration results in a working, testable piece
  • Continuous testing and quality assurance: testing throughout rather than at the end, for early detection

Choosing wrongly is expensive: the approach determines how requirements are gathered, how changes are managed, how risks are controlled and how the system is delivered, and the wrong one leads to cost overruns, delays, user dissatisfaction and system failure.

blocks.label: The five phases, their activities and their deliverables
blocks.tag: the densest thing in Module One
blocks.html:
PLANNING. Objectives: identify the scope of the new system, ensure the project is feasible, and develop a schedule, resource plan and budget. Five activities: define the problem; produce the project schedule; confirm project feasibility; staff the project; launch the project.

Feasibility comes in five kinds, and it belongs to PLANNING

Economic (cost-benefit), organisational, technical (technology and skills available), resource, and schedule (can it be done in time).
Elsewhere the manual lists it as technical, economic, operational, legal and schedule. Both lists appear; if asked, give the one the question's wording is closest to.

ANALYSIS. Objective: understand and document the business needs and processing requirements. Analysis is essentially a discovery process, and the key words are DISCOVERY and UNDERSTANDING. Six activities: gather information; define system requirements; prioritise requirements; build a prototype model for discovery; generate and evaluate alternatives; review recommendations with management.

Information is gathered by observing users at work, interviewing them, reading existing documents about procedures, business rules and job responsibilities, and reviewing existing automated systems.

DESIGN. Objective: design the solution system based on the requirements defined and decisions made during analysis.

High-level designLow-level design
An architectural structure for the software components, databases, user interface and operating environmentThe detailed algorithms and data structures required for software development

Five design activities: design the application architecture; design and integrate the network; design the user and system interfaces; design and integrate the database; design and integrate the system controls.

IMPLEMENTATION. Objective: produce a reliable, fully functional system and ensure all users are trained to use it. Five activities: construct software components; verify and test; convert data; train users and document the system; install the system.

Why testing matters more than it looks

The cost of bugs can be immense, and most organisations spend more time and attention on testing than on writing the programs in the first place.

SUPPORT. Objective: keep the system running productively for years after installation. Three activities: maintain the system (fixing bugs, minor adjustments), enhance it (major changes from new regulations, business environment, market opportunities, competition or infrastructure), and support the users through a help desk, which is the availability of support staff to assist with any technical or processing problem.

Deliverables by phase.

PhaseDeliverables
PlanningProject proposal and recommendation, investigation report, analysis of alternatives, cost and benefit analysis, schedule, recommendation
AnalysisDetailed system requirements, revised cost and benefits analysis, revised schedule
DesignLogical design, technical design, test plans, revised cost and benefits analysis, revised schedule
ImplementationSystem elements, implementation plans, contingency plans, end-user training materials, maintenance plan, operations plans, cutover or phase-in
SupportMaintenance reports, updated system documentation

blocks.label: The four conversion approaches
blocks.tag: installation means turning the old system off
blocks.html:
Installation is the process of turning off the old system and turning on the new one. Four ways to do it, and the exam wants them told apart.

ApproachWhat happensThe risk it manages
Direct cutoverThe new system immediately replaces the oldCheapest and fastest, and the most dangerous: no fallback
ParallelBoth systems run for a month or two until it is clear the new one has no bugsSafest, and the most expensive: everything is done twice
PhasedSmall parts of the new system gradually replace small parts of the oldSpreads risk over time, but the two must interoperate meanwhile
PilotA small group of users uses the new system before wider useLimits exposure to a few people rather than a few functions

Phased and pilot are the pair people confuse. Phased splits the SYSTEM. Pilot splits the USERS.

And whichever you choose, one of the most important aspects of conversion is developing a training plan to teach users the new system and help manage the change it introduces.

blocks.label: Every test question on this unit
blocks.tag: 10 of the sixty, answered and explained option by option

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
Four questions on test 1 gave four different SDLC phases as the four options and asked which one a description belonged to. If you can state each phase's OBJECTIVE in one line, those are free marks. If you only know the phase names in order, you will guess.

The other trap is where feasibility lives. It is a PLANNING activity, done before the project is committed to, not something done during analysis.

blocks.label: Drill every fact in this unit
blocks.tag: 63 questions from the course text, every option explained

blocks.big: "Planning, Analysis, Design, Implementation, Support. Predictive plans it all upfront; adaptive discovers it in sprints."
blocks.sub: Nine principles. Five feasibility types, in planning. Analysis is discovery and understanding. Design splits high-level from low-level. Testing takes more effort than programming. Four ways to convert: direct, parallel, phased, pilot.

lead: Nine principles, two approaches, and the five phases with everything each one produces.

title: Methodologies, and Choosing Between Them
blurb: Module One Unit 3. Waterfall and its two variants, RAD, incremental, both prototypings, Agile, and the six selection criteria. Half of test 1 came from here.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page, read a frame, answer, then slide down to check.

frames.teach: A system development methodology is the standard process an organisation follows to conduct all the steps necessary to analyse, design, implement and maintain information systems. It is a framework used to structure, plan and control development.
frames.ask: Is a methodology a process, a toolset, or a programming language?

frames.teach: Without one, development often leads to cost overruns, missed deadlines, and systems that fail to meet user and business requirements. Those three consequences come up again and again.
frames.ask: Name any three methodologies.

frames.teach: Waterfall is the traditional, linear approach where each phase must be completed before the next begins, proceeding sequentially like a natural waterfall.
frames.ask: What happens at the end of each Waterfall phase?

frames.check: the key deliverables are presented for approval.
frames.teach: Presented to the approval committee and project sponsor, before the project may move on. Strict monitoring comes from extensive written documentation, formal reviews, and user AND IT management sign-off at each phase end.
frames.ask: Waterfall has two very important variants. Name them.

frames.teach: Both keep Waterfall's structure and change one thing. Parallel changes WHEN work happens; V-Model changes when TESTING happens.

blocks.label: Waterfall: four advantages, six disadvantages, when to use it
blocks.html:
Advantages (4)Disadvantages (6)
Easy to understand, easy to useInflexible, slow, costly and cumbersome due to significant structure and tight controls
Provides structure to inexperienced staffForward-only progress with slight backward movement gives a false impression of progress
Sequential approach and strict controls ensure adequate documentation and design reviews, giving quality, reliability and maintainabilityLittle opportunity for the customer to preview the system, until it may be too late
Progress of development is measurableProblems are often not discovered until system testing
Difficult to respond to changes
Produces excessive documentation, time-consuming to keep updated
When to use Waterfall, seven conditions

Transaction-oriented batch system; project is large, expensive and complicated; clear objectives and a known solution; no pressure for immediate implementation; requirements clear and comprehensive; requirements stable throughout; and the team is inexperienced or may change during implementation.

That last one surprises people. The documentation carries the knowledge, so the model tolerates people leaving.

The manual also names the project types: government systems, financial applications, and regulatory or safety-critical systems.

blocks.label: The two Waterfall variants
blocks.html:
PARALLEL MODEL. Designed to reduce the long development time of strictly sequential phases, keeping the structured predictive nature but letting activities run simultaneously.

The detail that gets examined

The system is divided into subprojects AFTER the general analysis and high-level design phases are completed. Each subproject then runs detailed design, implementation and testing at the same time as the others, and they are integrated at the end.

Analyse once, design the shape once, then split. That is why the subprojects do not contradict each other.

V-SHAPE MODEL. V stands for VERIFICATION and VALIDATION. It keeps the sequential structure but establishes a direct relationship between each development phase and its corresponding testing phase. Development goes DOWN the left side of the V, testing comes UP the right side, so verification and validation are built in from the beginning rather than deferred to the end.

V-Model advantages (5)V-Model disadvantages (4)
Simple and straightforwardAffected by the rigidity of the waterfall model
Improves quality through early development of test plansDoes not easily handle dynamic changes in requirements
Management can track progress by milestonesDoes not suit the dynamic nature of the business environment
High quality deliverables because of test effectivenessDoes not contain risk analysis activities
Verification and validation done early in development

Use the V-Model when: the system requires high reliability, for example hospital patient control applications; all requirements are known up front; and the solution and technology are known.

blocks.label: RAD and the Incremental model
blocks.html:
RAD, Rapid Application Development, also called iterative development. It uses specialised techniques and computer tools to speed up analysis, design and implementation, so a portion of the system is developed quickly and delivered to users for evaluation and feedback. It emphasises reusable components, visual development tools and intensive user involvement, and reduces risk by breaking the project into smaller segments.

RAD tools: GUI builders, CASE tools, database management systems, fourth-generation programming languages, code generators, and object-oriented techniques.

RAD advantages (5)RAD disadvantages (5)
Focus moves from documentation to code (WYSIWYG)Users begin to work with a system that is intentionally incomplete, the chief disadvantage of iterative development
User feedback makes the model very effectiveMore speed and lower cost may lead to lower overall quality
Time-box approach mitigates cost and schedule riskUser expectations may increase and requirements expand: scope creep
Lower development cost because the system matches user expectationsRisk of never achieving closure, as expectations cannot be totally managed
Additional requirements identified and added to later versionsDevelopers and customers must commit to rapid-fire activities in an abbreviated time frame

Use RAD when: requirements are reasonably well known, the user will be involved throughout, technical risks are low, high performance is not required, and functionality is delivered in increments.

INCREMENTAL MODEL. Develops the system in small manageable portions called increments, each adding functionality and building on previous releases. It combines linear and iterative methodologies and sits between waterfall and prototyping.

The rule that catches people

Further requirements analysis can still be performed for LATER increments. But changes for the CURRENT increment cannot be accepted. That is what keeps each increment finishable.

Seven advantages: develop high-risk or major functions first; each release delivers an operational product; lowers initial delivery cost; divide-and-conquer breakdown; faster initial delivery; customers get important functionality early; reduced risk of changing requirements and project failure.

Five disadvantages: hard to map requirements to increments of the right size; hard to identify common facilities needed by all requirements; requires good planning and design; requires early definition of a complete and fully functional system so increments can be defined; requires well-defined module interfaces.

blocks.label: The two prototypings, and Agile
blocks.html:
Prototyping builds prototypes early to enable feedback. A quick and dirty version with minimal features is built, then reanalysed, redesigned and reimplemented after user reactions, and the cycle repeats until analysts, users and sponsor agree it has enough functionality to install. There are two types.

EVOLUTIONARYTHROWAWAY
What happens to itRefined and expanded until it BECOMES the final systemDISCARDED once requirements are clear
Also calledRapid or exploratory prototyping
PurposeDeliver a working system to end usersExplore design alternatives and clarify requirements
AnalysisStarts with the requirements best understoodA THOROUGH analysis phase comes first
Then whatThe prototype code is brought up to product standardThe real system is built with a structured methodology
Use whenRequirements evolve and rapid delivery is neededRequirements are unclear or users cannot articulate needs
RiskWeak architecture and difficult documentationTime spent on something you throw away

Evolutionary prototyping advantages: customers can SEE requirements as they are gathered; a more accurate product; unexpected requirements accommodated; developers learn from customers; flexible design and development; interaction stimulates awareness of additional needed functionality.

Evolutionary prototyping disadvantages: tendency to abandon structured development for code-and-fix; lack of careful methodical analysis before design decisions; a bad reputation for quick-and-dirty methods; overall maintainability may be overlooked; the customer may want the prototype delivered; and the process may continue forever, which is scope creep.

AGILE is a group of methods based on adaptive, iterative and incremental development, where every iteration is a complete software project. Modelling and documentation overhead is eliminated and face-to-face communication preferred. Work happens in short time-boxed sprints, each including requirement analysis, design, coding, testing and review, ending with a working increment delivered for feedback.

Agile activities: creation and prioritisation of user stories; sprint planning and task assignment; development and testing within each sprint; sprint review and retrospective.

The five popular agile methods, asked directly on test 1

Crystal Clear, Scrum, Extreme Programming (XP), Lean Software Development, Kanban.
The Critical Path Method is NOT one: it is a project scheduling technique.

blocks.label: The six selection criteria
blocks.tag: problem on the left, answer on the right
blocks.html:
The first challenge for a project manager is selecting the methodology, and no one methodology is always best. Six criteria, and this table is the single most examined thing in Module One.

CriterionWhat the manual says to use
Clarity of user requirements
Requirements unclear		System prototyping and throwaway prototyping, because they give users prototypes to interact with early in the SDLC
Familiarity with technology
Technology unfamiliar		Throwaway prototyping, because it explicitly encourages design prototypes for high-risk areas
System complexity
Complex system		Throwaway prototyping is well suited; system prototyping is NOT
System reliability
Reliability critical		Throwaway prototyping is most appropriate; the V-model is useful because it emphasises testing
Short time schedulesRAD, designed to accelerate development; iterative development and system prototyping let the team adjust functionality to meet a specific delivery date
Schedule visibilityRAD, which moves critical design decisions earlier so managers can recognise and address risks and keep expectations in check

Notice how often throwaway prototyping appears: four of the six. It is the manual's answer to almost any kind of UNCERTAINTY. RAD is its answer to TIME. The V-model is its answer to RELIABILITY when the question offers it.

Reliability examples: critical for medical equipment and missile control systems; merely important for games and internet video.

blocks.label: Every test question on this unit
blocks.tag: 15 of the sixty, answered and explained option by option

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
Reliability has two answers in the manual and only one is usually offered. Page 41 says throwaway prototyping is most appropriate when reliability is a high priority, AND that the V-model is useful when reliability is important. Test 1 Q30 offered the V-model and not throwaway prototyping, so the V-model was right. Read the options before deciding which sentence the examiner is quoting.

Second trap: the Parallel model and the V-model are both Waterfall variants and both get described as running things "at the same time". Parallel runs SUBPROJECTS at the same time. The V-model runs TESTING alongside development. Different things entirely.

blocks.label: Drill every fact in this unit
blocks.tag: 65 questions from the course text, every option explained

blocks.big: "Unclear requirements or unfamiliar technology, prototype it. Short schedule, RAD it. Lives at stake, V-model it."
blocks.sub: Waterfall is linear with sign-off gates. Parallel splits into subprojects after high-level design. V means verification and validation, down then up. RAD buys speed with a time box. Incremental combines linear and iterative. Evolutionary prototypes become the system; throwaway ones are discarded.

lead: Waterfall and its variants, RAD, incremental, both prototypings, Agile, and how to choose between them.

title: Requirements and Fact Finding
blurb: Module Two Unit 1. What a requirement is, the seven fact-finding techniques, interviews, JRP and the ethics.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page, read a frame, answer, then slide down to check.

frames.teach: Requirements discovery is the process and techniques used to identify and extract system PROBLEMS and solution requirements from the user community, with analyst and users working together.
frames.ask: The manual gives a precise definition of a problem. What is it?

frames.check: an undesirable situation preventing the organisation achieving its mission, vision, goals and objectives.
frames.teach: Notice how WIDE that is. Not a bug. Not lateness. Anything standing between the organisation and what it is trying to be. That breadth is why the analyst starts with the business rather than the software.
frames.ask: Requirements discovery has four activities. Name any two.

frames.check: problem discovery and analysis; requirements discovery; documenting and analysing requirements; requirements management.
frames.teach: System requirements are statements specifying what an information system should do and the conditions under which it must operate. They serve as a formal agreement between stakeholders and the development team.
frames.ask: Two types are identified. Name them.

frames.teach: The manual's shortcut is worth memorising word for word: functional requirements are what the system must DO; non-functional requirements are what it must HAVE. They are also called business requirements.
frames.ask: In which SDLC phase are system requirements developed?

frames.teach: And they provide the basis for design, implementation, testing and evaluation. Everything downstream rests on them, which is why getting them wrong is so expensive.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: the six results of incorrect requirements
blocks.html:
Six consequences, and the last one is about you

1. The system may cost more than projected
2. It may be delivered later than promised
3. It may not meet users' expectations, and that dissatisfaction may cause them not to use it
4. Once in production, the costs of maintaining and enhancing it may be excessively high
5. It may be unreliable, prone to errors and downtime
6. The reputation of the IT staff is tarnished, because any failure, regardless of who is at fault, will be perceived as a mistake by the team

Requirements discovery needs analytical, communication and interpersonal skills. Analysts must listen carefully, ask the right questions, resolve conflicting requirements, and validate findings with stakeholders to ensure accuracy and completeness.

blocks.label: The seven fact-finding techniques
blocks.tag: learn all seven, they are asked as a list
blocks.html:
Fact-finding is the formal process of using research, meetings, interviews, questionnaires, sampling and other techniques to collect information about system problems, requirements and preferences. It is also called information gathering or data collection.

TechniqueWhat it is
1. Sampling of existing documentation, forms and databasesReviewing organisation charts, memos, standard operating procedures, completed forms, screens and reports, database samples, and flowcharts
2. Research and site visitsLooking outside the organisation for how the problem is solved elsewhere
3. Observation of the work environmentThe analyst participates in or watches a person performing activities, to learn the system firsthand
4. QuestionnairesA special-purpose document collecting information and opinions from many respondents quickly and at low cost
5. InterviewsCollecting information from individuals through face-to-face interaction
6. PrototypingBuilding a small-scale, representative or working model of requirements to discover or verify them
7. Joint requirements planning (JRP)Highly structured group meetings to analyse problems and define requirements

Sampling documents gives insight into current business processes, business rules and information requirements, and reveals redundancies, inconsistencies and data quality issues.

Observation uncovers informal procedures, workarounds, bottlenecks and inefficiencies that users may not mention during interviews. That is its whole reason for existing: people describe the official process, not the real one.

Two questionnaire formats

FREE-FORMAT offers the respondent greater latitude: a question is asked and the answer is written in the space provided.
FIXED-FORMAT requires selecting from predefined responses. Its three types are multiple-choice, rating, and ranking.

Discovery prototyping is particularly useful when requirements are unclear or when user interface design is critical to success.

JRP is a SUBSET of JAD. Joint Application Development encompasses the entire systems development process; JRP is the requirements part of it. That relationship is worth remembering because the terms get used loosely everywhere else.

blocks.label: Observation, interviews and JRP in detail
blocks.tag: the procedures the exam asks you to list
blocks.html:
The nine observation guidelines. Six things to do and three not to.

DoDo not
Determine the who, what, where, when, why and howDo not interrupt the individuals at work
Obtain permission from appropriate supervisors or managersDo not focus heavily on trivial activities
Inform those observed of the purposeDo not make assumptions
Keep a low profile
Take notes during or immediately following
Review observation notes with appropriate individuals

Three of these protect the same thing, seeing work as it really is: do not interrupt, keep a low profile, get permission. Only note-taking is about you, and it exists because detail fades once you leave the room.

Two interview types, and two question types inside one of them

UNSTRUCTURED interview: conducted with only a general goal or subject in mind and few if any specific questions. The interviewer counts on the interviewee to provide a framework and direct the conversation.
STRUCTURED interview: the interviewer has a specific set of questions. Inside it, an OPEN-ENDED question lets the interviewee respond however seems appropriate, while a CLOSED-ENDED question restricts answers to specific choices or short direct responses.

Interviews can be used to: find facts, verify facts, clarify facts, generate enthusiasm, get the end-user involved, identify requirements, and solicit ideas and opinions.

The five-stage interview procedure: define the objective; select interviewees; prepare for the interview using an interview guide, which is a checklist of specific questions; conduct the interview; follow up on the interview by validating documented responses with the interviewee.

Communicating during it: approach with a positive attitude, set the other person at ease, let them know you are listening, ask questions, do not assume anything, take notes, and watch body language, the non-verbal information we communicate, including facial disclosure, eye contact and posture.

JRP participants: sponsor, facilitator, users and managers, scribes who take notes, and IT staff.

Planning a JRP session has three steps: select a location, away from the workplace when possible, needing several rooms with tables, chairs, whiteboard, projectors and computer equipment; select participants, each released from regular duties; prepare the agenda, with briefing documentation distributed beforehand.

Brainstorming, and the one rule that defines it

Brainstorming generates ideas by encouraging participants to offer as many as possible in a short period, WITHOUT ANY ANALYSIS until all the ideas have been exhausted. Only after everything is recorded are ideas analysed, evaluated, then refined, combined and improved.

Three benefits of JRP: it actively involves users and management, encouraging ownership; it reduces development time; and when it incorporates prototyping to confirm requirements and obtain design approvals, the benefits of prototyping are realised.

blocks.label: Ethics, and documenting what you found
blocks.html:
Fact-finding brings analysts into contact with company plans, employee salaries or medical history, and customer credit card or social security information.

Two duties, and they are not the same duty

1. Do not MISUSE the information. That is about you.
2. PROTECT it from people who would misuse it. That is about everyone else, and it is an active obligation rather than a courtesy.

Otherwise: the analyst loses respect, credibility and confidence of users and management, impairing the ability to do the job; the organisation and analyst could have legal liability; and the analyst could lose a job.

The Requirements Definition Document is a formal document communicating the requirements of a proposed system to key stakeholders, serving as a CONTRACT for the project. It is written in business language and gives a high-level description of functions and constraints. It is also called the requirements definition report, requirements statement, requirements specification, or functional specifications.

Three tools document draft requirements:

ToolWhat it is for
Use casesDescribe how actors interact with the system to achieve goals, focusing on what the system does from the user's perspective
Decision tablesRepresent complex business rules by listing all conditions and corresponding actions in a table, so every scenario is considered
Requirements tablesOrganise requirements with an ID, description, type, source, priority and status, so they can be tracked and validated

title: Use Cases: Diagram and Narrative
blurb: Module Two Unit 2. The four actor types, the five relationships, the narrative's seven parts, and how to build both from a scenario.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page, read a frame, answer, then slide down to check.

frames.teach: A use case represents how a system interacts with its environment, by illustrating the activities performed by the users and the system's responses.
frames.ask: Is a use case an internal or an external view of a business process?

frames.teach: The manual calls it an external or functional perspective: how users interact with the process, rather than its internal procedures or technical details.
frames.ask: Use-case modelling produces TWO outputs. Name them.

frames.check: the use case diagram and the use case narrative.
frames.teach: Marks are lost by naming only one. The diagram is the picture, giving a high-level view of the business events the system must process. The narrative is the text behind each use case.
frames.ask: What shape is a use case drawn as?

frames.check: an ellipse, with the name inside.
frames.teach: Use cases are triggered by external users called actors, drawn as stick figures. And here is the rule that decides most actor questions: actors are ALWAYS outside the system boundary.
frames.ask: So what separates the actors from the use cases on the diagram?

frames.teach: A rectangle, carrying the name of the system inside or on top, separating the system's internal use cases from external actors. Draw it every time; it is free marks and most people forget it.

blocks.label: The four actor types
blocks.html:
Actor typeDefinitionThe manual's example
Primary business actorPrimarily BENEFITS from the execution of the use case by receiving something of measurable or observable valueAn employee receiving a salary
Primary system actorDirectly INTERFACES with the system to initiate or trigger a business eventThe bursar who dispenses the cash
External server actorRESPONDS to a request from the use caseThe Financial Director approving the payment
External receiver actorNot the primary actor, but RECEIVES something of measurable value (output) from the use caseA warehouse receiving a packing order
Sort them with two questions

Primary or external? Does it drive the use case, or serve it?
Give or receive? Does it put something in, or take something out?

The pair that catches people is primary BUSINESS against primary SYSTEM. The business actor benefits; the system actor touches the keyboard. In the salary example they are two different people.

The five questions for finding actors, and actors are named with a NOUN or noun phrase:

  • Who or what provides input to the system?
  • Who or what receives output from the system?
  • Are interfaces required for other systems?
  • Are there any events automatically triggered at a predetermined time?
  • Who will maintain information in the system?

blocks.label: The five relationships
blocks.tag: and the arrow directions that get examined
blocks.html:
RelationshipMeaningNotation
Association
(communication)		Direct interaction between an actor and a use caseA simple line. WITH an arrowhead touching the use case: the actor at the other end INITIATED it. WITHOUT an arrowhead: interaction with an external server or receiver actor
ExtendsOptional or conditional behaviour extending a base use case under specific conditions; extracts complex functionality into its own use caseDashed arrow, FROM the extension TO the use case being extended
Include (uses)The base use case ALWAYS requires the other's behaviour; common functionality reused by several use cases, promoting reuse and avoiding duplicationDashed arrow, labelled with the include stereotype
Depends onOne use case cannot be performed until another has been. A change in one may affect the other, so it is valuable for managing change impactAn arrow between use cases
Generalisation
(inheritance)		Two or more actors share behaviour, so the shared part is extracted into a new ABSTRACT actor. Children inherit the parent's use cases and may add their ownA line with a TRIANGLE arrowhead
The extends arrow, which feels backwards until you read it aloud

"Generate Warehouse Packing Order EXTENDS Place New Member Order."
The arrow follows the sentence: from the extension, back to the base.

Contrast INCLUDE: "Record Grades INCLUDES Save Grades", always, every time. Include is ALWAYS. Extend is SOMETIMES. Both are dashed arrows, so the direction and the label are all you have.

The banking example, which the exam used twice. Customer is the abstract parent. Savings Account Holder and Current Account Holder both inherit Withdraw Money and Check Balance; only the Current Account Holder gets Request Overdraft. Separately, withdrawing cash depends on first depositing cash, and depositing cash depends on opening a bank account. Generalisation is about who HAS a use case; depends-on is about what must happen FIRST.

blocks.label: The use-case narrative
blocks.html:
The narrative is the textual description: how an actor interacts with the system to achieve a goal, step by step, without technical implementation detail.

PartWhat goes in it
Name and unique identifierShort text describing the action, such as Withdraw Money, plus a reference number
Actor(s)The people, systems or external entities that interact with the system
Description / GoalWhat the actor wants to achieve, summarising the purpose
PreconditionsConditions that must be true BEFORE it begins. If not met, the use case cannot proceed
Main flow (basic flow)The numbered step-by-step sequence between actor and system, describing the ideal scenario where everything works
Alternative flows (extensions)Variations, exceptions or error situations that branch off the main flow, such as an invalid PIN or insufficient funds
PostconditionsWhat must be true AFTER it completes, such as the account balance being updated

Read them as a story with bookends. Preconditions and postconditions are the before and after; main and alternative flows are what happens in between.

Why use cases matter, in the manual's three reasons: they identify and clarify functional requirements, and a well-developed use case diagram captures MOST of a system's functional requirements; they are very helpful for exceptions, special cases and error handling, which developers easily overlook; and the narrative is easy for users to read while flowing naturally into the process model and the data model.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.tag: buying glasses, from the patient's viewpoint
blocks.working:
Step 0, read the constraint. The question says from the view of the patient. So model only the patient's interaction. Every actor you invent beyond that loses marks rather than gaining them.

Step 1, identify business actors. Apply the five questions. Who provides input? The patient. Who receives output? The patient. So there is one actor: Patient.

Step 2, identify the use cases. Walk the scenario and take each thing the patient DOES:

  • Get Prescription
  • Select Frame
  • Place Order
  • Make Payment
  • Fitting and Adjustment

Step 3, construct the diagram. Draw the system boundary rectangle, put the five ellipses inside it, put the Patient stick figure outside on the left, and draw an association line from the Patient to each of the five.

Step 4, document the narrative. One per use case. Here is the manual's own, for Get Prescription:

Use Case NameGet Prescription
ActorPatient
DescriptionAllows the patient to obtain an eye prescription
PreconditionsPatient is registered or visits the clinic
Main Flow1. Patient requests eye test
2. System schedules and records test
3. Eye test is conducted
4. Prescription is generated
5. Prescription is provided to the patient
Alternative FlowTest unavailable, reschedule appointment
PostconditionsA valid prescription is issued

And Place Order, to show how preconditions chain:

PreconditionsValid prescription; Frame selected
Main Flow1. Patient confirms prescription and frame
2. System calculates cost
3. Patient confirms order
4. System creates order
Alternative FlowOrder cancelled by the patient
PostconditionsOrder is successfully created

Notice the pattern in every alternative flow: it is the one obvious thing that could go wrong at that step. Test unavailable. Frame not available. Order cancelled. Payment fails. If you are stuck for an alternative flow, ask what would stop this step, and write that.
blocks.problem: Create a set of use cases for the process of buying glasses from the viewpoint of the patient. First you see an eye doctor who gives you a prescription. Then you go to a glasses store, select your frames, and place your order. Once the glasses are made, you return to the store for a fitting and pay for them.

blocks.label: Every test question on this unit

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
Modelling as-is or to-be. AS-IS documents the current state, including processes, data flows, rules, users and technologies, without introducing assumptions or proposed solutions. TO-BE represents the desired future state after improvement. A question that says "the system currently..." wants as-is, and inventing improvements loses marks.

The four modelling steps in order: identify business actors, identify business requirements and use cases, construct the use-case model diagram, document the use-case narrative. Actors first, always, because actors determine the completeness of the requirements and can be used to verify and validate the use cases afterwards.

blocks.sub: Four actor types. Include is always, extend is sometimes, and the extends arrow points from the extension back to the base. Generalisation uses a triangle. Narrative runs name, actor, goal, preconditions, main flow, alternative flows, postconditions.

title: Process Modelling and Data Flow Diagrams
blurb: Module Two Unit 3. The four symbols, the three levels, balancing, the illegal flows and the three process errors. Twelve of test 2 came from here.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page, read a frame, answer, then slide down to check.

frames.teach: A process model is a graphical representation of how a business system should operate, showing the processes and activities performed and how data moves among them.
frames.ask: A process model can document two different systems. Which two?

frames.check: the AS-IS system (current) and the TO-BE system (new).
frames.teach: Modelling as-is helps identify inefficiencies, delays or redundancies, so the to-be model can enhance performance, reduce cost and increase productivity.
frames.ask: What is a MODEL, in one line?

frames.teach: Process modelling is a technique for organising and documenting a system's processes, inputs, outputs and data stores. Its main tool is the Data Flow Diagram.
frames.ask: What two questions does a DFD let the analyst answer?

frames.check: what does the organisation do, and how does the organisation do it.
frames.teach: But DFDs are purely logical, not physical models. They contain no implementation details, so no programming language, no hardware, no database product.
frames.ask: Why is the DFD drawn FIRST?

frames.check: so designers and users can concentrate purely on the business aspects.
frames.teach: The manual's phrase is that it is not contaminated by distractions of technical details. That is also why users who cannot read code can still check it.
frames.ask: How many DFD elements are there?

frames.teach: External agent, data flow, process, and data store. Learn the shape, the naming rule and the role of each, because the exam tests all three.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
ElementShapeNamed withWhat it is
External agent / entityRectangleA descriptive SINGULAR NOUNA person, organisation or system OUTSIDE the boundary that interacts with the system; source and destination of data. It does NOT perform processing
Data flowDirected arrow (a "pipe")NOUNS, connoting the actual informationData flows in packets through it; one arrow can represent the movement of multiple data items. Examples: Order Details, Receipt
ProcessRectangle with round edgesMust contain VERBS, must not be proceduralAn activity that transforms input data into output data. Data flowing out has more value after processing. A process is always active
Data storeOpen-ended rectangle (two parallel lines)Avoid verbs and physical descriptionsA place where data is stored for later use. Data never changes in the store except by a process reading it and returning updated data. Examples: Student Master, Client List
The phrase that separates two symbols

A data store is DATA AT REST. A data flow is DATA IN MOTION.
Going somewhere, it is a flow. Sitting somewhere, it is a store.

Naming a process, straight from the manual's own example:

WrongRightWhy
Add 1 to the counterIncrement counterThe first is PROCEDURAL, describing how a step is implemented. A DFD is a logical model, so it names business functions, not code

Six hints to identify a logical process. It performs computations; makes decisions; sorts, filters or summarises data; organises data into useful information; triggers other processes; or uses stored data, that is creates, reads, updates or deletes a record.

The notation above is Gane-Sarson. The other popular one is DeMarco and Yourdon. If a question names a notation, that is what it means.

blocks.label: The three levels, and balancing
blocks.html:
Decomposition is the iterative act of going from one single system to many component processes: breaking a complex system into smaller, more detailed sub-processes, so the analyst moves from a high-level overview to a detailed understanding.

LevelShowsThe rule that gets asked
Context Diagram
(Process 0)		The ENTIRE system as ONE single process, with data flows to and from external entitiesData stores are usually NOT included, unless owned by systems or processes other than the one being documented
Level 0 DFDThe major sub-processes, data flows AND data stores. It shows all the processes comprising the overall systemAll process models have EXACTLY ONE Level 0 DFD
Level 1 and lowerEach process broken into more detailed sub-processes, continuing until the process is simple enough to understandA Level 1 diagram explodes ONE process from Level 0, not the whole diagram
BALANCING, the single most examined DFD rule

When decomposing, you must CONSERVE the inputs and outputs of the process at the higher level. This is called balancing, and it ensures consistency across all levels.

Nothing may appear from nowhere in the child diagram, and nothing may vanish. Break it and your set of diagrams quietly describes more than one system.

The ATM example the manual works through. Context: one process, one entity, the Customer. Level 0: Authenticate User, Withdraw Money, Deposit Money, Check Balance, with data stores. Level 1: Withdraw Money explodes into Validate PIN, Check Balance, Dispense Cash.

blocks.label: Illegal flows and the three process errors
blocks.tag: one rule generates all of them
blocks.html:
The one rule

Every data flow must touch at least one PROCESS.
If both ends are non-process symbols, nothing is doing any work, and the flow is illegal.

Illegal flowThe fix
Data store to data storeInsert a process to MOVE the data from one store to the other
External agent to external agentInsert a process to EXCHANGE the data between the two boundaries
Data store to external agentInsert a process to RETRIEVE and PRESENT the data on the agent's behalf

And the legal ones, all of which touch a process: entity to process, process to store, store to process, process to entity, process to process.

The three named process errors. The names are pictures, so use them.

ErrorWhat is wrongPicture
Black holeInputs but NO outputs. Data enters and disappearsIt swallows
MiracleOutputs but NO inputs. Data is produced from nothingIt creates
Gray holeHas both, but the inputs are INSUFFICIENT to logically produce the stated outputsIt cheats

Black holes and miracles you spot by counting arrows. Gray holes you can only spot by thinking, which is why they are the commonest real fault and the one examiners like.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.working:
Step 1: the context diagram (Process 0). The whole system is one process. Read the scenario for entities: only the Customer is mentioned, so there is one.

Draw one rounded rectangle labelled ATM System, one plain rectangle labelled Customer, and arrows between them: in go card details, PIN, transaction request; out come cash, balance, receipt. No data stores, because none is owned elsewhere.

Step 2: the Level 0 DFD. Now break the single process into its major processes, and add the data stores.

  • 1.0 Authenticate User, reading from the Customer Account store
  • 2.0 Withdraw Money, reading and writing the Account store
  • 3.0 Check Balance, reading the Account store
  • 4.0 Print Receipt

Number them. Every arrow that crossed the boundary on the context diagram must still cross it here, going to or from one of these processes. That is balancing, checked for the first time.

Step 3: the Level 1 DFD. Pick ONE process and explode it. Take 2.0 Withdraw Money:

  • 2.1 Validate PIN
  • 2.2 Check Balance
  • 2.3 Dispense Cash

Number them as children of 2.0, which is what the decimal numbering is for.

Now check balancing, and say that you have

List the inputs and outputs of 2.0 Withdraw Money on the Level 0 diagram. Every one of them must appear on the Level 1 diagram, entering or leaving one of 2.1, 2.2, 2.3. Nothing extra crosses the edge.

Writing one sentence saying you have checked this is worth doing in an exam. It is the thing the examiner is looking for, and it costs you ten seconds.

A note on vocabulary while you are here. Making lunch is a BUSINESS PROCESS: a collection of activities producing a specific output for a particular customer. "Assemble sandwich ingredients" is a PROCESS: a specific ordering of work activities with a beginning, an end, and defined inputs and outputs. The business process is the whole job; a process is one ordered step inside it.
blocks.problem: A bank provides an ATM system that allows customers to perform basic banking transactions such as withdrawing cash, checking account balance, and printing receipts. Create a Process 0, Level 0 and Level 1 DFD for the user's interaction with the system.

blocks.label: Every test question on this unit
blocks.tag: 13 of the sixty, answered and explained option by option

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
"Only one Level 0" catches people, because it sounds plausible that a big organisation would have one per department. It would not: one system, one Level 0. Departments are not systems.

The context diagram comes FIRST, not last. It defines the scope everything else decomposes. An option saying Level 1 "precedes and determines" Level 0 is backwards.

blocks.tag: 32 questions from the course text, every option explained

blocks.big: "Every data flow must touch a process. Balance every level. Exactly one Level 0."
blocks.sub: Four symbols: agent rectangle, flow arrow, process round-edged rectangle, store open-ended rectangle. Store is data at rest, flow is data in motion. Black hole swallows, miracle creates, gray hole cheats.

title: Data Modelling and ER Diagrams
blurb: Module Two Unit 4. Entities, attributes, identifiers, relationships, the three cardinalities, and the five steps to draw one.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page, read a frame, answer, then slide down to check.

frames.teach: Data modelling is the analysis of data objects and the relationships between them. It is usually the first step in database design, and it produces an Entity-Relationship Diagram.
frames.ask: A DFD asks what the system does with data. What does an ERD ask?

frames.check: what data the system needs to keep, and how it is connected.
frames.teach: The manual puts it memorably: the DFD shows the VERBS of the system, and the ERD shows the NOUNS. Together they form the full requirements picture before a database is built.
frames.ask: Is a data model tied to a particular database product?

frames.check: no. It is independent of any database technology.
frames.teach: The same model could later be built in Microsoft Access, MySQL, or anything else, without changing the design. That is what makes it a requirements document rather than a technical one.
frames.ask: An ERD has four elements. Name them.

frames.teach: An ENTITY is a person, place, object, event or concept about which the organisation keeps data. Crucially, it always has more than one instance: one named student is not an entity, but Student is.
frames.ask: What shape, and singular or plural name?

frames.check: a rectangle, named with a SINGULAR noun.
frames.teach: Student, not Students, because the rectangle represents the whole category rather than any member of it.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: the four elements and their symbols
blocks.html:
ElementSymbolDefinition
EntityRectangleA person, place, object, event or concept the organisation keeps data about. Singular noun. Always more than one instance
AttributeOval, connected to its entityA piece of information captured about an entity, a property of it. Only include what the organisation needs, since every extra attribute is a column to store, validate and maintain
IdentifierThe attribute, markedThe attribute or combination that UNIQUELY identifies each instance. Also called the PRIMARY KEY
RelationshipA line, through a DIAMONDAn association between two or more entities, named with an ACTIVE VERB so the diagram reads like a sentence
What makes an identifier a GOOD identifier

It should never be blank, and it should never need to change once assigned.
That is exactly why systems use an assigned ID number rather than a phone number or email address: those change, and then every record pointing at them is wrong.

A COMPOSITE attribute breaks into smaller attributes of its own. Address may be composed of Street, City and State, drawn as smaller ovals branching off the Address oval.

A relationship line carries three properties, which together form the relationship statement:

  • The link phrase, the verb describing the relationship
  • The degree or cardinality, how many instances of one relate to instances of the other
  • The participation or ordinality, whether it is mandatory or optional

Benefits of data modelling: it clarifies exactly what data must be stored, reducing missing or duplicated information; it gives a stable foundation for physical design, since tables, columns and keys derive from it; it improves communication because the symbols are non-technical; and it exposes business rules and constraints before they are buried inside program code.

blocks.label: The three cardinalities, and ordinality
blocks.tag: the trickiest part of building an ERD
blocks.html:
CardinalityMeaningThe manual's example
One-to-one (1:1)Each instance of A relates to exactly one instance of B, and vice versaEach employee has one login account, each login account belongs to one employee
One-to-many (1:M)One A relates to many B, but each B relates back to only one AOne customer places many orders, each order belongs to one customer only
Many-to-many (M:N)Instances of A relate to many B, and instances of B relate to many AA student registers for many courses, a course has many students
What to do with a many-to-many

A many-to-many relationship is normally RESOLVED by introducing an ASSOCIATIVE ENTITY, such as Enrolment or Registration, when the ERD is converted into database tables.

If a question asks you to include "any associative entity needed", it is telling you a many-to-many is in there. Find it first.

ORDINALITY is the other half of the statement: whether the minimum number of instances required is zero (optional) or one (mandatory). A Student may be required to have at least one Enrolment, which is mandatory, while a Course might sit in the catalogue before anyone registers, which is optional.

Cardinality is about the MAXIMUM, ordinality about the MINIMUM. Together they say "at least this many, at most that many".

Read an ERD one line at a time, in BOTH directions. One Course Section has many Enrolments, each with its own grade, and each Enrolment applies to one Student. Read it back: one Student has many Enrolments, each with its own grade, and each applies to one Course Section. A database built from that produces grade lists one way and transcripts the other.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.tag: students and courses, the five steps
blocks.working:
Step 1: identify the entities. Read the scenario for nouns the organisation keeps data about. Here: Student and Course.

Step 2: identify the attributes, and mark the identifier.

StudentCourse
student_id (identifier)
name		course_code (identifier)
title

Step 3: identify the relationship, and name it with a verb. A student Registers for a course. Now the diagram reads as a sentence: Student Registers for Course.

Step 4: determine the cardinality. Ask it in both directions, one at a time.

  • Can one student register for many courses? Yes, so M.
  • Can one course have many students? Yes, so N.

Both directions many, so this is many-to-many.

Step 5: draw it. Two entity rectangles. A relationship diamond between them labelled Registers for. The cardinality letters M and N marked on either side of the diamond. Attribute ovals branching off each entity, with the identifier marked.

The habit that gets cardinality right every time

Never guess the pair. Ask two separate questions, one per direction:
"Can ONE of these have MANY of those?" Then "Can ONE of THOSE have MANY of these?"
Two yeses is M:N. One yes is 1:M, with the many on the yes side. No yeses is 1:1.
blocks.problem: A university wants to keep track of students and the courses they register for. Each student can register for many courses, and each course can have many students registered. Draw the ER diagram.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
This manual uses Chen notation. Relationship diamonds, attribute ovals, M and N labels. Not crow's foot. Draw what the manual draws.

Entity against attribute is a self-assessment question, so expect it. An entity has more than one instance and gets a rectangle; an attribute is a property of one and gets an oval. Student is an entity; student_name is an attribute. If you can imagine keeping a list OF it, it is an entity; if it is a column IN a list, it is an attribute.

title: Object Orientation and UML
blurb: Module Three Unit 1. Objects and classes, the three core concepts, the six design activities, and how UML is grouped.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: a different way of cutting up a system
blocks.howto: Cover the page, read a frame, answer, then slide down to check.

frames.teach: Everything so far kept process and data apart: DFDs modelled the processes, ER diagrams modelled the data, as two separate views. Object orientation combines them into a single unit called an object.
frames.ask: So what does an object hold that a DFD process does not?

frames.teach: An object is a single instance of something in the system, such as a particular student or a particular order. A running system, in this view, is just a set of objects sending messages to one another.
frames.ask: Every object has three things. Name any one.

frames.teach: STATE is the data it holds, represented as attributes. BEHAVIOUR is the operations it can perform, represented as methods. IDENTITY is what distinguishes it from every other object even if the attributes are identical.
frames.ask: Why is identity needed at all?

frames.check: two objects can have identical attributes and still be different things.
frames.teach: Two students could coincidentally share a name, but never a student ID. Identity is what the ID is standing in for.
frames.ask: What is a CLASS?

frames.check: the blueprint from which objects are created.
frames.teach: It defines the attributes and operations all objects of that type will have, but holds no data itself. The class Student says every student has a name and an ID and can register for a course; a particular student is an instance of it.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
ConceptWhat it meansThe manual's example
EncapsulationBundling an object's data and the operations acting on it together, and HIDING the internal details. Other parts interact only through defined operationsAnother module can call a Student's register() without knowing how it works inside
InheritanceOne class defined as a SPECIALISED version of another, avoiding repeating shared attributes and operationsPostgraduate Student inherits Student, adding its own attributes such as a supervisor
PolymorphismDifferent classes responding to the SAME operation call in ways appropriate to eachcalculateFee() works differently for an Undergraduate than a Postgraduate, though both are called the same way
A one-line hook for each

Encapsulation hides the inside.
Inheritance reuses the outside.
Polymorphism lets one call mean different things.

And notice what polymorphism buys: the rest of the system does not need to know which specific type it is dealing with. That is the point of it, and it is what an exam answer should say.

blocks.label: The design process, and how UML is grouped
blocks.html:
The six object-oriented design activities, in order:

  1. Identify the candidate classes, usually by examining the requirements model built during analysis, including the use cases
  2. Identify the relationships between classes: association, aggregation, composition, inheritance
  3. Identify the attributes and operations belonging to each class
  4. Model the classes and relationships in a class diagram
  5. Model how objects interact to fulfil each use case, typically using a sequence diagram
  6. Check that the classes identified are consistent with the use cases produced during requirements modelling

But they are ITERATIVE, not linear. Building a sequence diagram for a Register for Course use case might reveal a class needs an operation nobody listed, and that feeds back into step 3.

What UML is, and what it is NOT

The Unified Modelling Language is the industry-standard NOTATION for documenting object-oriented analysis and design.
UML is NOT a method. It is a common visual language that different object-oriented methods can use, in the way road signs are understood by drivers regardless of which driving school they attended.

STRUCTURAL diagramsBEHAVIOURAL diagrams
Describe the STATIC structure: the classes, objects and physical components, and how they relateDescribe how the system BEHAVES OVER TIME: how objects interact, how control flows, how objects change state
Class diagram
Component diagram
Deployment diagram		Use case diagram
Sequence diagram
Activity diagram
State chart diagram
Collaboration diagram

Three structural, five behavioural. The split to remember: if it could be a photograph, it is structural; if it needs a clock, it is behavioural.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: The use case diagram appears in both modules and is classified as BEHAVIOURAL. It was introduced in Module Two as a requirements tool, but Module Three counts it as a UML behavioural diagram, because it depicts how external agents interact with the system. If a question asks you to classify it, say behavioural.

title: Class Diagrams and Use Case Diagrams in UML
blurb: Module Three Unit 2. The three compartments, the four class relationships, include against extend, and both construction procedures.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page, read a frame, answer, then slide down to check.

frames.teach: A class diagram depicts the object structure of a system: the classes, their attributes and operations, and the relationships between them.
frames.ask: A class is drawn as a rectangle divided into how many compartments?

frames.teach: Name at the top, attributes in the middle, operations at the bottom. Everything you need to know about a class is visible in one shape.
frames.ask: There are four relationships between classes. What tells them apart on the page?

frames.check: the small symbol at one end of the line.
frames.teach: The manual says it plainly: they look similar because a line is a line. The symbol at the end is the whole difference, so drawing the right symbol is where the marks are.
frames.ask: Is a use case diagram structural or behavioural?

frames.teach: Even though it was introduced as a requirements tool in Module Two, UML classes it as behavioural, because it depicts how external agents interact with the system.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
RelationshipMeaningNotationThe manual's example
AssociationA general relationship: objects of one class connected to objects of anotherA line, often labelled with the multiplicity such as 1 or MOne Student associated with many Enrolment records
AggregationWhole-part, where the part CAN exist without the wholeHollow diamond at the whole endA Department has Lecturers, but a lecturer can transfer and still exist
CompositionStronger aggregation, where the part CANNOT exist without the wholeFilled diamond at the whole endAn Order is made of Order Lines; delete the order and its lines go too
Inheritance
(generalisation)		A SUBCLASS is a specialised version of a SUPERCLASS and inherits its attributes and operationsA line with a HOLLOW TRIANGLE pointing to the superclassPostgraduate Student specialising Student
Aggregation against composition, the pair that gets asked

Ask one question: if I delete the whole, does the part still make sense?

Delete the Department: the Lecturer still exists, and can transfer. That is AGGREGATION.
Delete the Order: an Order Line means nothing on its own. That is COMPOSITION.

The five steps to build a class diagram:

  1. Identify the candidate classes from the requirements model, particularly the use case diagram and narratives
  2. Identify the relationships and multiplicity between classes
  3. Identify the attributes of each class
  4. Identify the operations of each class
  5. Check the classes are consistent with the use cases already produced

In the worked example, Student and Course are the two main classes, and Enrolment is the ASSOCIATIVE CLASS needed because a student can register for many courses and a course can have many students. That is the same many-to-many resolution you met in the ERD unit, wearing an object-oriented hat.

blocks.label: Include against extend
blocks.html:
INCLUDEEXTEND
MeaningThe base use case ALWAYS requires the other to completeOptionally adds extra behaviour under certain conditions
ExampleRecord Grades includes Save Grades, since every act of recording must end with savingPlace Order extended by Apply Discount, but only when a discount code is entered
How oftenEvery timeSome of the time
Drawn asDashed arrowDashed arrow
They are BOTH dashed arrows

So the direction and the label are all you have. The everyday meaning of ALWAYS against SOMETIMES is the manual's own test, and it is the one to use in the exam.

The four steps to build a use case diagram:

  1. Identify the actors: the people or external systems that will use the system
  2. Identify the use cases: the tasks each actor needs to perform
  3. Draw an association line from each actor to every use case they are involved in
  4. Identify any include or extend relationships between use cases, drawn as dashed arrows labelled accordingly

The school grading worked example: actors are Teacher, Administrator and Student. Use cases are Record Grades, Update Grades, Distribute Report Cards, Generate Report Cards and View Grades. Record Grades and Update Grades both include Save/Load Grades, and View Grades includes Login, since a user must be logged in before grades can be viewed.

blocks.label: Every test question on this unit
blocks.tag: 1 of the sixty, answered and explained option by option

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: Login is an INCLUDE, not an extend. People reach for extend because logging in feels like a precondition rather than part of the job. But you must log in every time to view grades, and always means include. Ask how often, not how important.

blocks.big: "Three compartments. Aggregation the part survives, composition it does not. Include always, extend sometimes."
