title: The Behavioural UML Diagrams
blurb: Module Three Unit 3. Sequence, state chart, activity, component, deployment and collaboration diagrams, and when each is the right one.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page, read a frame, answer, then slide down to check.

frames.teach: A sequence diagram describes the flow of messages, events and actions between objects over time, showing how objects interact in one particular scenario of a use case.
frames.ask: What is the vertical dashed line under each object called?

frames.teach: Each object sits at the top of its own lifeline, and messages are drawn as horizontal arrows between lifelines, ordered top to bottom to show the sequence.
frames.ask: A solid arrow means one thing and a dashed arrow another. Which is which?

frames.check: solid is a call or request; dashed is a return or response.
frames.teach: So a glance at the arrow style tells you whether something is being asked for or handed back. That single convention earns marks on any sequence diagram question.
frames.ask: Where does time run on a sequence diagram?

frames.teach: Which is exactly what the collaboration diagram gives up, as you will see below. Time down the page is the sequence diagram's whole advantage.

blocks.label: The six diagrams, and what each is FOR
blocks.tag: choosing the right one is the exam question
blocks.html:
DiagramShowsKey notation
SequenceThe flow of messages between objects OVER TIME in one scenarioLifelines (vertical dashed), messages (horizontal arrows), solid for request, dashed for response, ordered top to bottom
State chart
(state machine)		The STATES an object passes through in its lifetime, and the EVENTS causing each moveStates as rounded rectangles, transitions as arrows labelled with the event, starting from a solid black circle
ActivityThe flow of CONTROL through the steps in a process. Similar in spirit to a flowchartActivity nodes, control and data flows, decision points as diamonds, parallel paths for simultaneous activities
ComponentThe physical architecture of the SOFTWARE: components and their dependenciesComponents, and the interfaces through which they provide services
DeploymentThe physical deployment of HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE: where each part runsProcessors, devices and software components, and the connections between them
Collaboration
(communication)		The same information as a sequence diagram, but organised SPATIALLY around the objectsObjects arranged in space, with messages NUMBERED to preserve order
The three comparisons the exam asks for by name

Sequence against collaboration: same information, different arrangement. Sequence organises by TIME down the page. Collaboration organises by STRUCTURE around the objects, numbering messages to keep the order. Use sequence when timing and order matter; use collaboration when how objects are structurally connected matters.

State chart against activity: a state chart tracks ONE OBJECT changing state. An activity diagram tracks a PROCESS flowing through steps. Order Placed to Confirmed to Shipped is a state chart; search, select, check availability, pay is an activity diagram.

Component against deployment: component is SOFTWARE architecture, deployment is HARDWARE. Component says which pieces the software is built from; deployment says which machines they run on.

A COMPONENT is a replaceable, self-contained part providing a defined set of services through one or more interfaces, and can be swapped for an alternative implementation as long as it honours the same interface.

The four steps to build a sequence diagram: identify the objects and place each at the top of its own lifeline; list the messages in the order they occur; draw each as a horizontal arrow at the right height, solid for request and dashed for response; number the messages if the order needs to be explicit.

The manual's worked examples: a sequence diagram for an ATM withdrawal with Customer, ATM System and Bank Server; a state chart for an Order going Placed, Confirmed, Shipped, Delivered, with a branch to Cancelled if the customer cancels or payment fails; an activity diagram for room booking with a decision point on availability; a deployment diagram with a client device over HTTPS to an application server, and over SQL to a database server.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: Not every object follows a straight line through its states. The Order example deliberately includes a Cancelled branch reachable from more than one state. If a state chart question gives you a scenario, include the failure path; a diagram with only the happy path is incomplete, and the manual makes that point explicitly.

blocks.label: Drill every fact in this unit
blocks.tag: 21 questions from the course text, every option explained

blocks.big: "Sequence is time down the page. State chart is one object changing. Activity is a process flowing. Component is software, deployment is hardware."
blocks.sub: Collaboration is a sequence diagram rearranged around the objects, with numbered messages. Lifelines are vertical dashed lines; solid arrows request, dashed arrows return; states are rounded rectangles from a solid black circle; decisions are diamonds.

lead: Six diagrams, and the three comparisons the examiner asks for by name.

title: Practical for Question One: Choosing and Justifying a Methodology
blurb: The Module One practical. A scenario, the answer worked in full, then two to attempt with model answers.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page, read a frame, answer, then slide down one line to check.

frames.teach: Module One has no diagrams, so its practical can only be a scenario and a judgement you must justify. Every one of the manual's own assignments has the same three parts.
frames.ask: Name the three parts, if you can guess them.

frames.teach: (a) IDENTIFY the most suitable approach. (b) JUSTIFY the choice against the scenario. (c) OUTLINE the key activities.
frames.ask: Which of the three carries the most marks?

frames.teach: Naming Agile earns almost nothing. The marks are in quoting the scenario back phrase by phrase and tying each phrase to a feature of the methodology.
frames.ask: A scenario says requirements will change frequently. Which criterion is that?

frames.check: clarity of user requirements, and it rules out a predictive approach.
frames.teach: One more habit worth the last mark: name the alternative you rejected and why. It shows the judgement the question is testing.

blocks.label: What the practical will look like
blocks.tag: read this before the worked one
blocks.html:
Module One has no diagrams, so its practical can only be one thing: a scenario, and a judgement you have to justify. The manual's own tutor-marked assignments confirm it. Page 26 sets a retail company and asks you to identify a suitable approach, justify the choice, and outline the key activities. Page 43 sets a clothing-line project and asks for skills, scope, team selection criteria, a methodology choice when requirements are unclear, and how to handle a client demanding features late.

The three-part shape, and it is always the same shape

(a) IDENTIFY the most suitable approach.
(b) JUSTIFY the choice, by explaining how it addresses the scenario's stated needs.
(c) OUTLINE the key activities that would be carried out.

Part (b) is where the marks are, and it is where most answers go thin. Naming Agile earns almost nothing. Quoting the scenario back and tying each phrase to a feature of the methodology is what earns the marks.

blocks.label: Worked practical
blocks.working:
Step 1: underline the scenario's signals before choosing anything. There are three, and the examiner put them there deliberately.

The scenario saysWhich criterion that is
"expects frequent changes in customer requirements"Requirements are unstable, so a predictive approach is ruled out
"plans to introduce new features regularly"Delivery must be incremental, not one big release
"seeks continuous user feedback throughout development"The user will be involved throughout the life cycle

Step 2: (a) identify. The ADAPTIVE approach, specifically an Agile methodology. Say both: the family and the member. If you prefer, RAD is defensible for the same reasons; what is not defensible is Waterfall or the V-model.

Step 3: (b) justify, phrase by phrase. This is the part worth writing carefully.

  • The company expects frequent changes. An adaptive approach assumes the project cannot be planned in full in advance and must be modified as it progresses, so change is accommodated by design rather than treated as a problem. A predictive approach defines requirements upfront and has limited flexibility to accommodate change, which is the opposite of what this company needs.
  • The company plans to introduce new features regularly. Agile works in short time-boxed sprints, each ending with a working increment of the system delivered for evaluation, so new features reach users continuously rather than waiting for a single delivery at the end.
  • The company seeks continuous user feedback. The adaptive approach is built on strong user involvement and collaboration, with requirements captured as user stories and prioritised by business value and urgency, and a sprint review and retrospective closing each cycle.
  • Retail is a dynamic business environment. The manual notes explicitly that adaptive approaches suit dynamic environments requiring flexibility and rapid response to change, while predictive approaches suit stable, well-understood requirements.

Step 4: (c) outline the key activities. Use the manual's adaptive phases, and name them.

  1. Initiation and requirements planning. Define high-level scope: the business problem, overall objectives, key stakeholders, major features. Detailed requirements are deliberately not fully specified. Requirements are captured at a high level as user stories and prioritised by business value and urgency.
  2. Iterative analysis and design. Only the requirements selected for the current iteration are analysed and designed in detail.
  3. Iterative development or construction. Components are built in short cycles, each producing a working, testable piece of the system.
  4. Continuous testing and quality assurance. Testing runs throughout rather than at the end, so defects are detected and corrected early.

Then, per sprint: create and prioritise user stories, plan the sprint and assign tasks, develop and test within the sprint, and hold a sprint review and retrospective.

How to earn the last few marks

Add one sentence saying what you would NOT do and why: a predictive approach such as Waterfall was rejected because its requirements are fixed upfront and it offers little opportunity for the customer to preview the system until it may be too late.

Showing the rejected alternative demonstrates the judgement the question is testing.
blocks.problem: A medium-sized retail company wants to develop a new online sales and inventory management system. The company expects frequent changes in customer requirements, plans to introduce new features regularly, and seeks continuous user feedback throughout development. As a systems analyst: (a) identify the most suitable software development approach; (b) justify your choice; (c) outline the key activities that would be carried out using this approach.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: You are the project manager for a new clothing line. The requirements of the work MAY NOT be clearly stated at the beginning. Choose an appropriate SDLC methodology and map the project's phases. Then: near the end, the client insists on adding new features, and you want to prevent scope and feature creep. Do you agree or refuse? Give three reasons.
blocks.answer:
Methodology. Requirements unclear at the start points straight at the selection criterion clarity of user requirements, and the manual's answer there is system prototyping or throwaway prototyping, because they provide prototypes for users to interact with early in the SDLC. Since a clothing line also implies visual design that people must react to rather than describe, evolutionary prototyping fits: build an initial version, refine it through continuous user feedback until it becomes the final product.

Phases mapped. A preliminary project plan; a partial high-level model as a source for partial requirements; a prototype built with the basic and critical attributes; the designer builds the database, user interface and algorithmic functions; demonstrate, the user evaluates and suggests improvements; loop until satisfied, then bring the prototype up to product standard.

On the late feature request. Either answer can score, provided the reasons are the manual's. A defensible refusal:

  • Scope creep is a named risk of exactly this methodology. The manual lists among prototyping's disadvantages that the process may continue forever due to scope creep, and that user expectations may increase and requirements expand during the project.
  • There is a risk of never achieving closure, since user expectations cannot be totally managed. Accepting late features feeds that risk directly.
  • The principle allows revising scope deliberately, not drifting into it. Do not be afraid to cancel or revise scope is about a controlled decision when a project is too costly or misaligned, which is not the same as absorbing requests near delivery.

A defensible acceptance would cite the incremental model instead: accept the features into a LATER increment, since further requirements analysis can still be performed for later increments, while changes for the current increment cannot be accepted. That answer scores because it names the mechanism rather than just saying yes.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: A teaching hospital wants a patient monitoring system for its intensive care unit. All clinical requirements have been specified in advance by the medical board and are not expected to change. The system must be highly reliable, since failures could endanger patients. Identify the most suitable methodology, justify it, and state one significant disadvantage the hospital should plan for.
blocks.answer:
Identify. The V-Shape Model.

Justify, against the manual's three conditions for it, all three of which the scenario satisfies:

  • The system requires high reliability. The manual's own example is hospital patient control applications, which is this scenario almost word for word. V stands for verification and validation, and the model pairs every development phase with a corresponding testing phase, so verification and validation are built in from the beginning rather than deferred to the end.
  • All requirements are known up front, stated here by the medical board. That removes the objection that would normally count against a predictive model.
  • The solution and technology are known, as this is an established clinical application area.

Add the quality argument: the V-model improves overall quality through early development of test plans, and gives high quality deliverables because of test effectiveness.

One significant disadvantage to plan for. Any of the four scores: it is affected by the rigidity of the waterfall model; it does not easily handle dynamic changes in requirements; it does not suit a dynamic business environment; or, the strongest one to name here, it does not contain risk analysis activities, which for a safety-critical system is a real gap the hospital would need to cover separately.

blocks.big: "Identify, justify, outline. And justify by quoting the scenario back, phrase by phrase."
blocks.sub: Unclear requirements or unfamiliar technology, prototype. Short schedule, RAD. High reliability with fixed requirements, V-model. Large, stable and complicated with no time pressure, Waterfall. Name the rejected alternative too.

lead: Identify, justify, outline. A scenario worked in full, then two to attempt.

title: Practical for Question Two: Drawing Use Cases, DFDs and ERDs
blurb: The Module Two practical. Three artefacts, each worked from a scenario, then scenarios to attempt.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: which artefact, and the habit that earns marks
blocks.howto: Cover the page, read a frame, answer, then slide down one line to check.

frames.teach: Module Two contains three drawable things, so question 2 will ask for one of them.
frames.ask: Name all three.

frames.check: a use case diagram, a DFD, an ERD.
frames.teach: The manual sets assignments on all three: a sports centre for use cases, a restaurant and a car rental for ERDs, and the ATM for DFDs. So rehearse all three.
frames.ask: The manual gives a numbered procedure for each. Why does that matter in the exam?

frames.check: because an examiner marking to a scheme is looking for those steps.
frames.teach: So write the steps down as headings and answer under each. A correct diagram with no working scores less than a correct diagram with its five steps labelled.
frames.ask: After drawing a levelled DFD, what should you always write one sentence about?

frames.check: that you have checked the balancing.
frames.teach: Every input and output of the parent process still accounted for among the children. It costs ten seconds and it is the thing the examiner is looking for.

blocks.label: Which artefact will they ask for
blocks.html:
Module Two contains three drawable things, so question 2's practical is one of three. All three are worth rehearsing, because the manual's assignments set all three: a sports centre booking system for use cases, a restaurant and a car rental company for ERDs, and the ATM for DFDs.

The habit that earns marks on any of them

Write the steps down as headings and answer under each. The manual gives a numbered procedure for every artefact, and an examiner marking to a scheme is looking for those steps. A correct diagram with no working scores less than a correct diagram with its five steps labelled.

blocks.label: Worked practical A
blocks.tag: a use case diagram, the sports centre
blocks.working:
Step 1: identify the actors. Apply the five questions. Who provides input? The customer, and the admin. Who receives output? Both. Are interfaces required for other systems? Payment is mentioned, so a Payment Gateway is defensible as an external server actor. Notification is sent, so a Notification Service is defensible as an external receiver actor.

Safe answer: Customer and Staff/Admin. Stronger answer: add Payment Gateway as an external server actor, since it responds to a request from the use case.

Step 2: identify the use cases. Take each thing an actor DOES, as a verb phrase.

CustomerStaff/Admin

Make Booking

Step 3: draw association lines. System boundary rectangle labelled Sports Centre Booking System. Customer stick figure outside on the left, Staff/Admin outside on the right. A line from each actor to each of their use cases.

Step 4: identify include and extend. This is where the marks separate.

  • Make Booking INCLUDES Check Availability. Every booking checks availability, so it is always. Include.
  • Make Booking INCLUDES Make Payment. The scenario says the customer confirms then proceeds to payment, and the booking is only confirmed once payment succeeds. Always. Include.
  • Make Booking INCLUDES Send Confirmation Notification, since the system sends it after every successful reservation.
  • View, Modify and Cancel Booking each INCLUDE Log In, since the customer must be logged in first. This mirrors the manual's own grading example, where View Grades includes Login.
Where people lose marks here

Making Log In an extend. It is not optional, so it is an include. Ask how often, not how important.

And forgetting the system boundary rectangle entirely. It is one line on the page and it is explicitly part of the notation.

When booking, the system displays available time slots; the customer selects a date and time, confirms the booking, and makes payment. Once payment succeeds the booking is confirmed and recorded, and the system sends a confirmation notification. Customers can also view, modify or cancel bookings. The extra mark almost nobody takes

blocks.problem: A restaurant wants to keep track of Customers and the Orders they place. A customer can place many orders, but each order belongs to one customer. Each order contains one or more Menu Items, and a menu item can appear on many orders. Identify the entities, list at least three attributes for each with the identifier marked, and draw the complete ER diagram showing all relationships and their cardinality.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: A car rental company wants to track Customers and the Vehicles they rent. A customer can rent many vehicles over time, and a vehicle can be rented by many different customers over time, but never by more than one customer at once. Identify all entities including any associative entity needed to record each individual rental, list at least three attributes for each with identifiers, and state the cardinality and ordinality of every relationship.
blocks.answer:
Entities. Customer, Vehicle, and the associative entity Rental. The scenario hands you the associative entity in the phrase "to record each individual rental", and the many-to-many between Customer and Vehicle is why it is needed.

CustomerVehicleRental
customer_id (identifier)
name
licence_number
phone_number		vehicle_id (identifier)
registration_number
make_and_model
daily_rate		rental_id (identifier)
start_date
return_date
total_cost

Relationships and cardinality. Introducing Rental splits the many-to-many into two one-to-many relationships, which is exactly what an associative entity is for:

  • Customer Makes Rental: one customer makes many rentals, each rental belongs to one customer. 1:M.
  • Vehicle Appears In Rental: one vehicle appears in many rentals over time, each rental is for one vehicle. 1:M.

Ordinality, which the question asks for explicitly and most answers skip:

  • A Rental must have a customer and must have a vehicle: mandatory, minimum one, on those sides.
  • A Customer may exist having rented nothing yet, and a Vehicle may sit on the forecourt unrented: optional, minimum zero, on those sides.

The clause about never more than one customer at once is a business rule about non-overlapping dates rather than a cardinality. Say so in a sentence: it constrains the start and return dates of rentals for the same vehicle, and would be enforced as a business rule rather than shown by the cardinality notation. Naming a constraint the notation cannot express is exactly the judgement the question is probing.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: A college library lets members search the catalogue, borrow books and return them. Borrowing checks the member's record for unpaid fines and updates the loans record. Librarians add new books to the catalogue and produce overdue reports. Draw the context diagram and the Level 0 DFD, then decompose Borrow Book to Level 1.
blocks.answer:
Context diagram (Process 0). One rounded rectangle, Library System. Two external agent rectangles: Member and Librarian. Flows in: search query, borrow request, returned book, new book details. Flows out: search results, loan confirmation, overdue report. No data stores, since none is owned by another system.

Level 0. Major processes, numbered, plus the stores:

  • 1.0 Search Catalogue, reading the Catalogue store
  • 2.0 Borrow Book, reading Catalogue and Member, writing Loans
  • 3.0 Return Book, writing Loans
  • 4.0 Add New Book, writing Catalogue
  • 5.0 Produce Overdue Report, reading Loans and Member

Data stores: Catalogue, Member, Loans. Note that every store is written by at least one process and read by at least one; a store nothing writes to is a sign you have missed a process.

Level 1, decomposing 2.0 Borrow Book:

  • 2.1 Verify Member, reading the Member store
  • 2.2 Check Unpaid Fines, reading the Member store
  • 2.3 Check Book Availability, reading the Catalogue store
  • 2.4 Record Loan, writing the Loans store

Then balance it, and say so. 2.0 took in a borrow request and gave out a loan confirmation, reading Catalogue and Member and writing Loans. On the Level 1 diagram the borrow request enters 2.1, the loan confirmation leaves 2.4, and the same three stores are touched. Nothing new crosses the edge and nothing has disappeared.

Check for the three errors before you hand it in. Does every process have at least one input and one output? No black holes, no miracles. Could each process's inputs plausibly produce its outputs? No gray holes. And does every flow touch a process? No store talking to an agent directly.

1. Candidate classes from the use cases: Guest, Room, Booking, Payment. Manager is arguably an actor rather than a class; include it if you also model staff data.

2. Relationships and multiplicity:

  • Guest makes Booking: 1 to M, one guest many bookings
  • Booking is for Room: M to 1, many bookings over time for one room
  • Booking has Payment: 1 to 1

3. Attributes and 4. operations, in the three-compartment box:

(b) The sequence diagram, in four steps.

1. Objects, each on its own lifeline, left to right: Guest, Booking System, Payment Gateway.

2 and 3. Messages, top to bottom, solid for a request and dashed for a response:

  2. Booking System to Guest: availableRooms  dashed
  3. Guest to Booking System: selectRoom(room)  solid
  4. Guest to Booking System: confirmBooking()  solid
  5. Booking System to Payment Gateway: requestPayment(amount)  solid
  6. Payment Gateway to Booking System: paymentConfirmed  dashed
  7. Booking System to Guest: bookingConfirmation  dashed

(d) The state chart for a Booking object. Start at a solid black circle, states as rounded rectangles, arrows labelled with the triggering event:

  • Created, on booking submitted
  • Confirmed, on payment succeeds
  • Checked In, on guest arrives
  • Completed, on guest checks out
  • Cancelled, reachable from Created or Confirmed, on guest cancels or payment fails
Include the failure path

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: A student logs into a course portal and views their results. Draw a sequence diagram for this interaction. Then state which UML diagram you would use instead if you wanted to show how a Result object moves from Draft to Published to Archived, and why.
blocks.answer:
Sequence diagram. Three objects, three lifelines: Student, Course Portal, Results Database.

  1. Student to Course Portal: login(username, password)  solid
  2. Course Portal to Results Database: verifyCredentials()  solid
  3. Results Database to Course Portal: credentialsValid  dashed
  4. Course Portal to Student: loginSuccess  dashed
  5. Student to Course Portal: viewResults()  solid
  6. Course Portal to Results Database: fetchResults(student_id)  solid
  7. Results Database to Course Portal: resultsData  dashed
  8. Course Portal to Student: displayResults  dashed

Time runs down the page, so the order is carried by the heights. Solid arrows are requests, dashed are returns.

Which diagram for Draft to Published to Archived, and why. A state chart diagram, because it shows the different states an object can be in during its lifetime and the events that cause it to move between them. The three named things are STATES of a single Result object, not steps in a process, and a state chart is for objects whose behaviour depends heavily on their current state.

An activity diagram would be wrong here: it shows the flow of control through the steps of a PROCESS, like a flowchart. The distinction to state in the answer is one object changing state, against one process flowing through steps.

blocks.big: "One scenario, many diagrams. Ask what the question is really about: an object changing, a process flowing, or software and hardware sitting."

Answer · PQ 25/26 Q1

a. Entity-relationship diagram (4.5 marks)

The nouns kept as records are LANDLORD, HOUSE, AGENT, SUPERVISOR (the tenant) and PAYMENT. The relationships from the story: a landlord owns many houses; an agent manages many houses; an agent serves a supervisor; a supervisor occupies a house; a supervisor makes payments; an agent forwards payments to the landlord.

Answer, continued

b. Data flow diagrams (9 marks)

Context diagram: one process "0 Rental system" in the middle, with SUPERVISOR and LANDLORD as external entities. Flows: supervisor sends "house request" and "rent payment" in; the system sends "house availability" back to the supervisor and "forwarded payment" to the landlord. Level 0: explode process 0 into the major processes: 1.0 Match tenant to house, 2.0 Agree and clean, 3.0 Collect and forward rent. Add data stores D1 Houses and D2 Payments. Wire the flows so each process has an input and an output, and so the "house request" in and "forwarded payment" out still match the context diagram (balance).

Level 1 of process 3.0 (rent payment): explode 3.0 into 3.1 Receive payment from supervisor, 3.2 Record payment (to D2 Payments), 3.3 Forward payment to landlord. The total flows in and out (payment in, forwarded payment out) balance process 3.0.

Answer, continued

c. Three more reasons to succeed and three to fail (3 marks)

Succeed (besides customer acceptance): clear and agreed requirements; strong user involvement throughout; a realistic schedule and budget with good project management.

The bar at the Customer end means "one" and the circle-with-crow's-foot at the Order end means "zero or many". So, forward chaining: one CUSTOMER places zero or many ORDERs. Backward chaining: each ORDER is placed by one and only one CUSTOMER.

Answer · PQ 25/26 Q3

a. Three feasibility questions (3 marks)

Feasibility analysis asks whether the project is worth pursuing, from three angles: Is it technically feasible? (do we have the technology and skill to build it?); Is it economically feasible? (do the benefits outweigh the costs?); and Is it operationally feasible? (will the users accept and use it, and does it fit the business?). Schedule and legal feasibility complete the five, but these three are the core questions.

b. Six more problem-solving steps (3 marks)

After researching and understanding the problem: verify the benefits outweigh the costs; define the requirements; develop alternative solutions; recommend the best solution; define the details of the chosen solution; implement it (and then monitor the results).

c. Explaining what a model is (4 marks)

Tell the stakeholders a model is a simplified picture of the system that leaves out detail so everyone can see and agree the important parts before it is built, the way an architect's drawing lets a client approve a building before a brick is laid. The use case diagram, DFD and class diagram they will be shown are all such models.

d. Another skill (3 marks)

Besides people skills, Billy needs technical knowledge and skills: an understanding of computers, networks, databases and the tools and techniques of system building, so he can understand and communicate technical requirements even though the programmer writes the code. Maintain the system (fix bugs and make minor adjustments); enhance the system (add capability as the business grows); and support the users, which includes running a help desk.

Project manager, software architect, and product designer (also acceptable: software tester, business analyst).

Answer · PQ 25/26 Q5

a. Compare seven methodologies (7 marks)

  • Waterfall: strong documentation and traceability suit a safety-critical system, but its rigidity is risky if requirements shift.
  • Prototyping: good for the unclear priorities here, but the prototype can be mistaken for the finished safety system.
  • RAD: fast, which suits the twelve-month deadline, but weak for a large, complex, safety-critical hospital system.
  • Spiral: its risk analysis each cycle fits a safety-critical project well, but it is heavy and slow.
  • Incremental: delivers working pieces early, useful given the deadline, but integration across departments must be managed.
  • Agile: handles the disagreeing stakeholders through constant feedback, but its light documentation clashes with the audit-trail requirement.
  • V-shape: pairs each stage with its test, excellent for the reliability and traceability a hospital demands, but as rigid as waterfall.
Answer, continued

b. Five project planning activities (5 marks)

Define the problem; produce the project schedule; confirm feasibility; staff the project; and launch the project.

c. Formulate requirements (5.5 marks)

  • Business: cut medication-administration delays; achieve regulatory compliance with full audit trails.
  • User: a nurse can administer and record medication at the bedside; a doctor can see a complete patient record in one place.
  • Functional: the system shall record each patient appointment; the system shall flag duplicated laboratory test requests; the system shall log every change to a record for audit.
  • Non-functional: the system shall be available 99.9% of the time; the system shall encrypt all patient data (privacy).
  • System: the system shall store records as time-stamped entries linked to a patient ID; the system shall integrate with the existing departmental applications.

a. As-is, to-be and assumptions (3.5 marks)

As-is weaknesses: no single platform, so learning is unsupported; no automated feedback or plagiarism checking; no analytics for administrators. To-be improvements: one platform teaching three languages with automated feedback, debugging support, plagiarism alerts and analytics. Assumptions to validate: that 8,000 students across three campuses have reliable network access; that the platform can integrate with the existing learning management system; that the AI feedback is accurate enough to be trusted.

b. Elicitation plan (4 marks)

  • Interview lecturers: information on the learning outcomes and marking rules; suitable because they hold the academic requirements and can be probed in depth.
  • Questionnaire to students: information on what help they want; suitable because it cheaply reaches 8,000 scattered students.
  • Observation of a lab session: information on how students really code and get stuck; suitable because it shows real behaviour.
  • Document review of the learning management system: information on existing data and integration points; suitable because it grounds the design in what exists.

c. Short notes on UML (2 marks)

UML is a standard set of diagram notations for modelling object-oriented systems, created by Booch, Rumbaugh and Jacobson. Its uses: to visualise, specify, construct and document a software system in one shared language.

d. Two categories of UML diagram (4 marks)

Structural diagrams model what the system is: the class diagram (classes and relationships) and the object diagram (objects at a moment). Behavioural diagrams model what it does: the use case diagram (what users can do) and the activity diagram (a process flow); the sequence diagram is another.

e. Four class relationships (4 marks)

Inheritance (hollow triangle, is-a): a Postgraduate is a Student. Composition (filled diamond, life-or-death has-a): an Order is made of Order Lines. Aggregation (hollow diamond, loose has-a): a Department has Lecturers who survive it. Association (plain line): a Doctor treats a Patient. Draw the four side by side as Figure 5.2 in Module Five.

Answer · PQ 24/25 Q1

a. Two elicitation techniques (4 marks)

Interview the head librarian: suitable because they hold the borrowing rules and can be probed in depth; advantage, rich detailed information; limitation, slow and only a few people. Questionnaire to student borrowers: suitable because it cheaply reaches the large, scattered student body; advantage, wide reach at low cost; limitation, no follow-up and often a low response rate.

b. Requirements and a reason (6.5 marks)

Functional: the system shall let a member borrow a book; shall let a member reserve a book; shall calculate and record fines. Non-functional: the system shall respond within two seconds; shall be available 99.9% of the time; shall keep member data secure. Reason for multiple levels: different levels (a student, a librarian, a head of library) use the system differently, so gathering from all of them captures needs that a single level would miss.

c. Methodology and scope creep (7 marks)

i. Unclear requirements call for an adaptive method: choose prototyping or RAD, which discover requirements as they go. Map the phases: plan, then build a prototype, review it with the client, refine, and repeat until the requirements settle, then implement and support. ii. Refuse (or defer) the new features, because they threaten the agreed schedule and budget, they risk the quality of the nearly finished system, and they should be handled as a change request or a later release.

a. Four phases: objectives and activities (8 marks)

Analysis: objective, understand and document what the system must do; activities, gather information, define and prioritise requirements, build prototypes, evaluate alternatives. Design: objective, specify how it will be built; activities, design the architecture, network, interfaces, database and controls. Implementation: objective, a reliable working system with trained users; activities, construct, test, convert data, train and document, install. Support: objective, keep it running for years; activities, maintain, enhance, support the users (help desk).

b. Three stakeholders (3 marks)

Users want it easy and helpful for daily work; managers want business value on time and on budget; developers want clear requirements and a feasible, maintainable system.

c. Tools versus techniques (4 marks)

A tool is a software product used to do the work; a technique is a way of completing one activity. Tools: a modelling package, an IDE. Techniques: interviewing, cost-benefit analysis.

The business goals and processes, the people and their roles, the data the business keeps, the existing systems and their weaknesses, and the rules and constraints the new system must respect.

Answer · PQ 24/25 Q3

a. DFD elements (2 marks)

External entity, process, data store, data flow.

b. Data store (1.5 marks)

A data store is data at rest in the system, a file or table where data is held between processes. It is named with a noun (for example D1 Stock), never a verb, and given a store number.

c. Reading Figure 1 (3 marks)

Read each relationship both ways from its crow's-foot marks. For example: one CUSTOMER makes many SALEs, and each SALE is made by one CUSTOMER (1:M); one CUSTOMER is targeted by many TARGETED PROMOTIONs, and each promotion targets many customers (M:N); a CUSTOMER adds many CUSTOMER FAVORITEs (1:M); an AVAILABLE TUNE is included in many CUSTOMER INTERESTs (M:N). State the cardinality (one or many, optional or mandatory) for each line the figure draws.

Answer, continued

d. Warehouse ERD and Level 0 DFD (9.5 marks)

ERD: entities TRUCK DRIVER, TRUCK, MANAGER, LABORER, STOREKEEPER, STOCK, STOCK REPORT, ACTIVITY REPORT. A TRUCK DRIVER submits many TRUCKs; a TRUCK may carry zero or many STOCK (optional); a LABORER unloads many TRUCKs; a STOREKEEPER takes inventory of STOCK and generates STOCK REPORTs; drivers and labourers submit ACTIVITY REPORTs to the MANAGER. Crow's foot throughout, with the optional (circle) mark on the truck-to-stock line.

Level 0 DFD: external entities TRUCK DRIVER and MANAGER; processes 1.0 Receive and unload truck, 2.0 Take inventory, 3.0 Generate stock report, 4.0 Submit activity report; data stores D1 Stock and D2 Reports. Wire the flows so each process has input and output, and balance them against the context diagram.

e. Validate the diagrams (1.5 marks)

Check every process has both an input and an output (no black holes or miracles); check no illegal flow (every flow touches a process); and check the levels balance (the flows in and out of a process match its explosion).

Answer · PQ 24/25 Q4

a. Four reasons to model (2 marks)

A model is a clear picture non-technical users can check; it separates what the system does from how it is built; it shows the system boundary and everything it touches; and it breaks a large system into manageable processes.

b. Cardinality, optionality, data balancing (5.5 marks)

i. In crow's foot: one-to-one (a bar at each end), one-to-many (a bar at one end, a crow's foot at the other), many-to-many (a crow's foot at each end); draw each on a line between two entity rectangles. ii. A relationship is optional when the minimum is zero, drawn with a circle on the line (a customer may have zero orders). iii. Data balancing means the data flowing into and out of a process on a parent diagram must match the data flowing into and out of its child diagram when it is exploded.

c. Process modelling versus data modelling (1.5 marks)

Process modelling (DFD)Data modelling (ERD)
Shows data in motionShows data at rest
Built from processes and flowsBuilt from entities and relationships
Answers how data movesAnswers what data is stored
Answer, continued

d. Sales management ERD (3 marks)

Entities SALES REP, CUSTOMER, ORDER, PRODUCT, WAREHOUSE. SALES REP serves zero-or-many CUSTOMERs, each CUSTOMER served by one rep; CUSTOMER places one-or-many ORDERs, each ORDER by one customer; ORDER contains one-or-many PRODUCTs; WAREHOUSE stores zero-or-many PRODUCTs. Mark the optional (circle) and many (crow's foot) ends as the words say.

e. Data cannot move between entities (1 mark)

A data flow must touch a process at one end, so you cannot draw an arrow straight from one external entity rectangle to another: put a process bubble between them. For example, Customer to Bank is wrong; Customer to "1.0 Process payment" to Bank is right.

f. Researcher ERD (3 marks)

Entities RESEARCHER, INSTITUTION, RESEARCH INTEREST. A RESEARCHER belongs to one INSTITUTION (many researchers per institution, so INSTITUTION 1:M RESEARCHER); a RESEARCHER has many RESEARCH INTERESTs (1:M, or M:N if interests are shared). Crow's foot with the one bar at the institution end.

With only one month, buy a packaged solution or outsource, not build. Factors: the very short time available, the lack of in-house build capacity in the time, and that a hospital admin system is not so unique that a package cannot fit.

Answer · Mock 1 · Q5

title: The Last Hour, on One Page
blurb: Every list the examiner has asked for, in the order you will meet them.

blocks.label: Module One, the lists
blocks.html:
Analyst's problem-solving, 8 steps: understand the problem, verify benefits outweigh costs, define requirements, develop alternatives, decide and recommend, define details, implement, monitor.

Analyst's 7 roles: requirements analysis, system evaluation, feasibility studies, system modelling and documentation, liaison, solution recommendation, support during development and implementation.

9 principles: get the user involved; use a problem-solving approach; establish phases and activities; establish standards; justify systems as capital investments; do not be afraid to cancel or revise scope; divide and conquer; design for growth and change; proper planning and project management.

5 SDLC phases: Planning, Analysis, Design, Implementation, Support. Support is in the SDLC but not in the initial project.

Feasibility, 5 kinds: economic, organisational, technical, resource, schedule. Elsewhere: technical, economic, operational, legal, schedule. It is a PLANNING activity.

Analysis, 6 activities: gather information, define requirements, prioritise requirements, build a prototype for discovery, generate and evaluate alternatives, review recommendations with management. Key words: discovery and understanding.

Design, 5 activities: application architecture, network, user and system interfaces, database, system controls. High-level is architecture; low-level is algorithms and data structures.

Implementation, 5 activities: construct components, verify and test, convert data, train users and document, install.

Support, 3 activities: maintain, enhance, support users via help desk.

4 conversions: direct cutover, parallel, phased, pilot. Phased splits the SYSTEM, pilot splits the USERS.

6 selection criteria: clarity of user requirements, familiarity with technology, system complexity, system reliability, short time schedules, schedule visibility.

5 agile methods: Crystal Clear, Scrum, XP, Lean, Kanban. NOT the Critical Path Method.

blocks.label: Module Two, the lists
blocks.html:
7 fact-finding techniques: sampling documentation, research and site visits, observation, questionnaires, interviews, prototyping, JRP.

Requirements discovery, 4 activities: problem discovery and analysis, requirements discovery, documenting and analysing, requirements management.

6 results of incorrect requirements: costs more, delivered later, does not meet expectations so is not used, high maintenance costs, unreliable and prone to downtime, IT staff reputation tarnished.

2 ethical duties: do not misuse the information; protect it from those who would.

4 DFD elements: external agent (rectangle, singular noun), data flow (arrow, noun), process (round-edged rectangle, verb, not procedural), data store (open-ended rectangle, no verbs).

3 DFD levels: context (whole system as one process, no data stores unless owned elsewhere), Level 0 (major processes plus stores, exactly ONE per system), Level 1 (explodes one process).

3 process errors: black hole (in, no out), miracle (out, no in), gray hole (inputs insufficient for outputs).

3 illegal flows: store to store, agent to agent, store to agent. Every flow must touch a process.

4 actor types: primary business (benefits), primary system (interfaces to trigger), external server (responds), external receiver (receives output, not primary).

5 use case relationships: association, extends (arrow from extension to base), include (always), depends on (order), generalisation (triangle).

7 narrative parts: name and ID, actors, description, preconditions, main flow, alternative flows, postconditions.

4 ERD elements: entity (rectangle, singular), attribute (oval), identifier (primary key), relationship (diamond, active verb).

3 cardinalities: 1:1, 1:M, M:N. M:N resolved by an associative entity. Cardinality is the maximum; ordinality the minimum, meaning optional or mandatory.

blocks.label: Module Three, the lists
blocks.html:
3 things every object has: state (data), behaviour (operations), identity.

3 core concepts: encapsulation (hides the inside), inheritance (reuses), polymorphism (one call, many behaviours).

6 design activities: candidate classes, relationships, attributes and operations, class diagram, sequence diagram, check against use cases. Iterative, not linear.

UML grouping. Structural: class, component, deployment. Behavioural: use case, sequence, activity, state chart, collaboration. UML is a NOTATION, not a method.

4 class relationships: association (line, multiplicity), aggregation (part survives the whole), composition (part dies with the whole), inheritance (hollow triangle to the superclass).

Class diagram, 5 steps: classes from the use cases, relationships and multiplicity, attributes, operations, check against use cases. Three compartments: name, attributes, operations.

Use case diagram, 4 steps: actors, use cases, association lines, include and extend.

Sequence diagram, 4 steps: objects on lifelines, messages in order, arrows (solid request, dashed response), number if needed. Time runs DOWN.

The three comparisons: sequence organises by time, collaboration by structure with numbered messages. State chart tracks one OBJECT changing; activity tracks a PROCESS flowing. Component is SOFTWARE; deployment is HARDWARE.

blocks.label: The traps, all in one place
blocks.html:
• Analysis says WHAT, design says HOW. What must be defined first.
  • Interpersonal skills are the analyst's MOST important skills. Not technical.
  • Feasibility belongs to PLANNING, not analysis.
  • Parallel splits subprojects; V-model runs testing alongside. Both are Waterfall variants.
  • The Parallel split happens AFTER general analysis and high-level design.
  • Evolutionary prototypes BECOME the system; throwaway ones are DISCARDED.
  • Reliability has two manual answers: throwaway prototyping is most appropriate, the V-model is useful. Read the options before choosing.
  • Exactly ONE Level 0 DFD per system. Not one per department.
  • The context diagram comes FIRST.
  • Process names must be verbs and must not be procedural. Add 1 to the counter is wrong; Increment counter is right.
  • The extends arrow points FROM the extension TO the base.
  • Include is ALWAYS, extend is SOMETIMES. Login is an include.
  • Actors are ALWAYS outside the boundary, and the boundary rectangle must be drawn.
  • An entity always has more than one instance, and is named with a singular noun.
  • This manual uses Chen notation: diamonds and ovals, not crow's foot.
  • The use case diagram is classed as BEHAVIOURAL.
  • Aggregation the part survives; composition it does not.
  • Include the failure path on a state chart.
